Week 4 Overview

The Purpose of This Week

Weeks 1–3 built your ADM knowledge from the ground up. By now you can trace an architecture initiative through all 9 phases, name every formal input and output, explain governance, and apply key techniques.

Week 4 fills the remaining structural gaps:

  • Enterprise Continuum — the classification system TOGAF uses to store and reuse architectures
  • Reference Models — TRM and III-RM in full detail (both appear on the exam by name)
  • Views and Viewpoints — how architecture is communicated to different stakeholders (operationalized, not just defined)
  • Content Framework — the complete picture of what every ADM phase actually produces
  • Synthesis — a unified mental model that connects all 7 TOGAF parts

Without this week's content, you know the process of TOGAF but not its structural foundations — and roughly 30–35% of exam questions test exactly these structural topics.

Day 1: Enterprise Continuum — Full Deep Dive (Part V)

What the Enterprise Continuum Is

The Enterprise Continuum is defined in Part V of TOGAF 9.2 as:

A view of the Architecture Repository that provides methods for classifying architecture and solution artifacts — both internal and external to the Repository — as they evolve from generic Foundation Architectures to Organization-Specific Architectures.

In plain English: the Enterprise Continuum is a classification and organization system for everything architecture-related, arranged on a spectrum from the most generic (applies to any organization) to the most specific (applies only to this organization).

Why this matters: Organizations waste enormous effort redesigning solutions that have already been designed. The Enterprise Continuum ensures that every time an architecture is created, it is classified, stored, and made available for reuse by future projects. It is TOGAF's mechanism for institutional architectural memory.

The Two Continua

The Enterprise Continuum consists of two parallel continua — this is the most commonly missed detail. Most students know the spectrum (Foundation → Common Systems → Industry → Organization-Specific) but don't know there are two separate tracks:

Track 1 — Architecture Continuum: A spectrum of architecture designs from generic to specific
Track 2 — Solutions Continuum: A spectrum of implementations (products, services, systems) from generic to specific

These two tracks are parallel and aligned — for every level of the Architecture Continuum, there is a corresponding level in the Solutions Continuum:

GENERIC ◄──────────────────────────────────────────────────────► SPECIFIC

Architecture    Foundation      Common       Industry      Organization-
Continuum:      Architecture    Systems      Architecture  Specific
                                Architecture               Architecture
                    ↕               ↕            ↕              ↕
Solutions       Foundation      Common       Industry      Organization-
Continuum:      Solutions       Systems      Solutions     Specific
                                Solutions                   Solutions

                [MOST REUSABLE]                          [LEAST REUSABLE]
                [MOST GENERIC]                           [MOST SPECIFIC]
Exam tip

Know that the Enterprise Continuum has TWO parts: Architecture Continuum (designs) and Solutions Continuum (implementations). This distinction is frequently tested. A common wrong answer is "the Enterprise Continuum has one track that goes from generic to specific."

The Architecture Continuum — 4 Levels in Detail

Level 1: Foundation Architecture

  • The most generic level — applies to ALL organizations everywhere
  • Describes the fundamental architecture building blocks that any IT system requires
  • Does NOT describe any specific technology — just what categories of capability are needed
  • TOGAF provides its own Foundation Architecture: the Technical Reference Model (TRM) and the Foundation Architecture principles
  • Example: Any enterprise needs capability for: data management, security, network communication, transaction processing, user interface
  • Used by: anyone; the starting point for all architecture work

Level 2: Common Systems Architecture

  • Built on top of Foundation Architecture
  • Captures patterns that are common across many organizations but not all
  • Describes architectures that appear repeatedly across industries
  • Examples:
    • Security Architecture (how authentication, authorization, and encryption are managed)
    • Systems Management Architecture (how IT systems are monitored and managed)
    • Communications Infrastructure Architecture (how enterprise communications work)
    • Integration Architecture (how systems connect to each other)
  • Used by: organizations that adopt industry best practices; patterns available from standards bodies, The Open Group, and vendor communities

Level 3: Industry Architecture

  • Built on Common Systems Architecture
  • Captures patterns specific to a particular industry vertical
  • Examples:
    • Banking: Core Banking Reference Architecture (accounts, transactions, customers, products)
    • Healthcare: HL7 FHIR reference architecture for health data exchange
    • Government: e-Government reference architectures
    • Retail: Retail industry reference architecture
    • Telecommunications: TM Forum Frameworx
  • Used by: organizations within the specific industry; available from industry consortia, standards bodies, and professional associations
  • In Saudi context: Vision 2030 digital government reference architectures, SAMA (Saudi Central Bank) banking architectures

Level 4: Organization-Specific Architecture

  • Built on top of industry architectures
  • Captures the specific, unique architecture of one particular organization
  • This is the architecture that most organizations think of as "their enterprise architecture"
  • Includes all organization-specific customizations, integrations, and extensions
  • Example: Saudi Aramco's specific data architecture, incorporating industry oil and gas patterns but tailored to Aramco's specific operations, systems, and regulations
  • Used by: only that specific organization
Exam tip

The direction of reuse is always LEFT to RIGHT (generic to specific). When starting an architecture, you look LEFT for what can be reused. When you've created something useful, it moves LEFT over time (organization-specific → industry → common systems) as others adopt it.

The Solutions Continuum — 4 Levels in Detail

The Solutions Continuum mirrors the Architecture Continuum but contains implementations rather than designs:

Foundation Solutions: Generic products and services implementing Foundation Architecture

  • Operating systems (Windows, Linux)
  • Basic networking equipment (routers, switches)
  • Standard database engines (PostgreSQL, Oracle)
  • Apply to any organization

Common Systems Solutions: Products implementing Common Systems Architectures

  • Security platforms (identity management systems, SIEM tools)
  • Systems management tools (monitoring platforms, service desk systems)
  • Integration middleware (message brokers, API gateways)
  • Apply to many organizations across industries

Industry Solutions: Industry-specific products

  • Core Banking Systems (Temenos, Finastra, SAP Banking)
  • Electronic Health Record systems (Epic, Cerner)
  • Telecommunications BSS/OSS systems (Amdocs, Ericsson)
  • Apply only within the specific industry

Organization-Specific Solutions: Custom or configured implementations

  • Organization's specific ERP configuration (SAP configured to Aramco's exact needs)
  • Custom-built internal applications unique to the organization
  • Apply only to that specific organization

Architecture Continuum vs Solutions Continuum — The Key Distinction

Architecture Continuum Solutions Continuum
Contains Architecture designs, models, principles, patterns Products, systems, services, implementations
Nature Conceptual and prescriptive Concrete and descriptive
Question answered "What should the architecture look like?" "What implements this architecture?"
Example at Industry level Core Banking Reference Architecture (design) Temenos T24 Core Banking System (product)
Use in ADM Reference during Phases B, C, D for design guidance Reference during Phases E, F for implementation selection
Created by Architects designing architectures Vendors, integrators, developers building solutions
Exam tip

Architecture Continuum = DESIGNS. Solutions Continuum = IMPLEMENTATIONS. An exam question might describe a scenario and ask which continuum it belongs to. If it's a reference architecture, framework, or design pattern → Architecture Continuum. If it's a product, system, or deployed solution → Solutions Continuum.

Architecture Partitioning

Architecture Partitioning is the concept of dividing a large enterprise architecture into manageable segments that can be developed and governed independently while remaining consistent.

A single monolithic enterprise architecture covering an entire large organization is unmanageable. Partitioning allows parallel work by different teams on different parts.

Dimensions of Partitioning:

1. By Level (Architecture Landscape): Already covered in Week 2 — Strategic, Segment, and Capability architectures:

  • Strategic Architecture: Enterprise-wide, long-term capability roadmap
  • Segment Architecture: Architecture for a specific business unit, function, or geography
  • Capability Architecture: Architecture for an enabling shared capability (security, data management, integration)

2. By Domain:

  • Business Architecture partition
  • Data Architecture partition
  • Application Architecture partition
  • Technology Architecture partition

Each domain can have its own architecture team working in parallel, as long as they remain coordinated.

3. By Time Horizon:

  • Short-term architecture (next 12 months)
  • Medium-term architecture (1–3 years)
  • Long-term architecture (3+ years)

4. By Geography:

  • Regional architecture (e.g., EMEA architecture)
  • National architecture (e.g., Saudi Arabia operating model)
  • Global enterprise architecture

Rules for Partitioned Architectures:

  1. A lower-level architecture (e.g., Segment Architecture) must be consistent with the higher-level architecture (e.g., Strategic Architecture)
  2. Partitioned architectures must be integrated at defined integration points
  3. Architecture governance must span all partitions — the Architecture Board has authority over all
Exam tip

Architecture Partitioning is about managing complexity in large organizations. The key rule: lower-level architectures (Segment, Capability) must be consistent with the Strategic Architecture above them. Multiple ADM cycles can run simultaneously on different partitions.

Enterprise Continuum and the Architecture Repository

The Architecture Repository (Part V, 6 layers) stores architectures organized by the Enterprise Continuum:

Architecture Repository Storage by Continuum Level:

Layer 5: Reference Library
├── Foundation Architectures (TRM, Foundation Architecture)
├── Common Systems Architectures (security, management patterns)
└── Industry Architectures (banking, healthcare, government)

Layer 3: Architecture Landscape
├── Strategic Architecture (org-specific, long-term)
├── Segment Architectures (org-specific, by business unit)
└── Capability Architectures (org-specific, enabling)

Layer 4: Standards Information Base
└── Technology standards (common systems and org-specific)

The more generic (Foundation, Common Systems, Industry) architectures live in the Reference Library. Organization-Specific architectures live in the Architecture Landscape.

How Organizations Use the Enterprise Continuum

Practical Example: A Saudi Commercial Bank Implementing a New Digital Banking Platform

  1. Start with Foundation Architecture: What categories of capability does any banking platform need? (Security, data management, transaction processing, user interface, network services) — from TRM

  2. Look at Common Systems Architectures: How do organizations generally implement API gateways, identity management, and integration platforms? — from Reference Library

  3. Look at Industry Architectures: What does a banking digital architecture look like? (Core banking, channels, risk management, regulatory reporting) — from banking industry reference architectures like BIAN (Banking Industry Architecture Network)

  4. Add Organization-Specific elements: This bank's specific products, its regulatory requirements in KSA (SAMA compliance), its legacy systems to integrate, its specific customer segments

  5. Store the result: The bank's organization-specific architecture is stored in the Architecture Landscape. The useful patterns are contributed back to the Reference Library for future reuse.

Exam tip

The Enterprise Continuum supports reuse by giving architects a structured place to look for existing solutions before designing from scratch. "If you've solved it, store it. If someone has already solved it, reuse it."

Key Takeaway for Day 1 (Enterprise Continuum)

The Enterprise Continuum has TWO parallel tracks: the Architecture Continuum (designs, from Foundation → Organization-Specific) and the Solutions Continuum (implementations, same 4 levels). Architecture Partitioning divides large enterprises into manageable segments. The Enterprise Continuum connects to the Architecture Repository: generic architectures in the Reference Library; organization-specific architectures in the Architecture Landscape.

Day 2: Foundation Architecture, Technical Reference Model (TRM), and III-RM (Part VI)

What Part VI Is

Part VI of TOGAF 9.2 contains the TOGAF Reference Models — pre-built example architectures that organizations can use as starting points. These are concrete examples of the Foundation Architecture level of the Architecture Continuum.

TOGAF provides two reference models:

  1. Technical Reference Model (TRM) — a taxonomy and graphical model of generic technology services
  2. Integrated Information Infrastructure Reference Model (III-RM) — a reference model for integrated enterprise information infrastructure

Both TRM and III-RM are Foundation Architecture artifacts — they are completely generic and apply to any organization. Organizations are expected to use them as starting points and then customize for their specific context.

🔟 10th Edition note (important for OGEA-101 candidates): In the TOGAF Standard, 10th Edition, the TRM and III-RM were removed from the core/Fundamental Content and relocated to a separate "Reference Models" Series Guide. They are not part of the OGEA-101 Foundation exam syllabus. If you are sitting OGEA-101, read this day for conceptual understanding (the layered "what technology services exist" idea is still useful background), but do not invest heavy memorisation time here — redirect that time to the ADM, ADM Techniques, Applying the ADM, Governance, and Architecture Content, which carry the marks. If you are sitting the legacy TOGAF 9 Foundation exam, study this day fully (~5–8% weight).

The Foundation Architecture

The Foundation Architecture is the most generic level of the Architecture Continuum. TOGAF defines it as:

An architecture that provides the most generic context for the other architectures. It provides a foundation upon which more specific architectures can be built.

The Foundation Architecture consists of:

  • Architecture Principles — the most generic governance rules (established in Preliminary Phase)
  • Technical Reference Model (TRM) — the generic technology taxonomy
  • Standards Information Base — references to generic technology standards

When an organization starts using TOGAF, they start with the Foundation Architecture (particularly the TRM) and build upward toward their organization-specific architecture.

Technical Reference Model (TRM) — Full Coverage

What the TRM Is

The TRM is TOGAF's generic reference model for technology. It provides:

  1. A taxonomy — a classification system for ALL technology services that any enterprise might use
  2. A graphical representation — a layered diagram showing how technology components relate

The TRM is used primarily in Phase D (Technology Architecture) as the vocabulary for identifying what technology components are needed and how they relate.

TRM Graphical Representation

The TRM diagram is typically drawn as a layered architectural diagram:

  • Top layer: Application Software (the applications users interact with)
  • Middle layer: Application Platform (the technology services that applications use — the largest section)
  • Bottom layer: Communications Infrastructure (the network, hardware, and communications technology)
  • Side panel: Quality of Service attributes that apply across all layers

The key insight of the TRM diagram: everything depends on the layer below it. Applications depend on platform services. Platform services depend on communications infrastructure. This layering is the fundamental concept of technology architecture.

How the TRM is Used in ADM

Phase D (Technology Architecture):

  1. Architect references the TRM taxonomy to ensure all required technology service categories are considered
  2. For each TRM category, the architect identifies: what exists today (AS-IS) and what is needed (TO-BE)
  3. The organization's specific technology choices populate the TRM categories to create the Technology Reference Architecture (organization-specific version of TRM)
  4. Technology Standards Matrix is built from the technology choices made

Example — Using TRM in Phase D:

TRM Category: Security Services
→ AS-IS: Password-based authentication, basic firewall
→ TO-BE: Multi-factor authentication, Zero Trust security model, SIEM platform
→ Gap: Implement MFA, deploy SIEM, redesign network segmentation
→ Standards: Microsoft Entra ID for identity, Splunk for SIEM
Exam tip

The TRM has two main components: (1) a taxonomy of technology services, and (2) a graphical representation (the layered diagram). Know both. Exam question: "What does the TOGAF TRM provide?" → A taxonomy of technology services and a graphical representation showing how they relate.

III-RM (Integrated Information Infrastructure Reference Model) — Full Coverage

What the III-RM Is

The III-RM is TOGAF's second reference model. Unlike the TRM (which classifies technology services generically), the III-RM represents a specific architecture pattern: how to build an integrated enterprise information infrastructure — an environment where all enterprise systems share information and work together.

TOGAF defines the III-RM as:

A reference model that supports the vision of Boundaryless Information Flow — a world where data and information can flow without barriers to those who need it, when they need it, wherever they are.

"Boundaryless Information Flow" is a key TOGAF/Open Group concept: the idea that information should flow freely and securely across organizational and system boundaries.

Exam tip

This distinction is tested. TRM = taxonomy of what technology services exist. III-RM = blueprint for how to integrate those services into an enterprise information infrastructure. A question might say "which reference model is used to design integrated application infrastructure?" → III-RM.

Where TRM and III-RM Fit in Enterprise Continuum

Both TRM and III-RM are Foundation Architecture elements:

  • They are the most generic — they apply to any organization
  • They sit at the leftmost end of the Architecture Continuum
  • Organizations use them as starting points and add organization-specific elements to the right

In the Architecture Repository, TRM and III-RM are stored in the Reference Library (Layer 5).

Key Takeaway for Day 2 (Reference Models)

TRM = taxonomy of technology service categories + layered diagram. Used in Phase D. Classifies technology into Application Software, Application Platform (with many sub-services), and Communications Infrastructure. III-RM = blueprint for integrated enterprise information infrastructure. Used in Phases C and D. Both are Foundation Architecture artifacts at the most generic end of the Architecture Continuum, stored in the Reference Library of the Architecture Repository.

Day 3: Architecture Views and Viewpoints — Full Treatment

The Foundation Standard: ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010

TOGAF's entire view and viewpoint model is based on ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010:2011 — the international standard for "Systems and Software Engineering — Architecture Description."

This standard established that:

  1. A complex system has many stakeholders, each with different concerns
  2. No single representation can address all concerns effectively
  3. An architecture description must provide multiple views — each addressing specific concerns
  4. Viewpoints are the mechanisms for creating consistent, repeatable views

TOGAF adopts this framework and applies it to enterprise architecture. When you work with views and viewpoints in TOGAF, you are implementing an internationally standardized approach.

Exam tip

ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010 is the international standard underlying TOGAF's view/viewpoint model. This appears in exam questions: "Which international standard is the basis for TOGAF's architecture views and viewpoints?" → ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010.

The Full Chain — Deepened

Week 1 introduced the chain. Now we operationalize it:

STAKEHOLDER
    │
    │ has one or more
    ▼
CONCERN (what they care about in the architecture)
    │
    │ is addressed by selecting a
    ▼
VIEWPOINT (a specification for constructing a view —
           defines: purpose, audience, what aspects to show,
           what notations to use, quality criteria)
    │
    │ is applied to the architecture description to produce a
    ▼

      that addresses one or more concerns from a viewpoint)
    │
    │ is expressed using one or more
    ▼
ARTIFACT (the tangible output: diagram, matrix, catalog, table, model)

Important nuances:

  • One stakeholder can have multiple concerns → multiple viewpoints → multiple views
  • One viewpoint can be applied to different architectures → creates different views each time
  • One view can address multiple concerns (if they are related)
  • A viewpoint is a TEMPLATE — the same viewpoint produces a different view for different architectures

Viewpoints — What They Formally Define

A Viewpoint is not just "a way of looking at something." In TOGAF (following ISO 42010), a Viewpoint formally specifies:

Viewpoint Component Description Example
Name Identifying label "Security Architecture Viewpoint"
Concerns What stakeholder concerns this viewpoint addresses Data confidentiality, system integrity, access control
Stakeholders Who this viewpoint is designed for CISO, Security team, Audit team
Notation What modeling notation is used UML component diagram with security annotations
Operations What types of operations can be performed on this view Analysis, design, simulation
Correspondence rules How this view relates to other views Must be consistent with the Application Architecture View

When an architect uses a viewpoint to create a view, they are following all these specifications. This ensures that views are created consistently across different projects and architects.

One Viewpoint → Many Views

A single viewpoint can generate many different views. This is a key concept that is frequently misunderstood:

Example: The "Data Flow Viewpoint"

  • Concerns: Data movement, data transformation, data ownership, latency
  • Stakeholders: Data architects, data stewards, integration teams
  • Notation: Data Flow Diagram (DFD) notation

Applied to the Order Management domain → creates: "Order Processing Data Flow View" Applied to the Customer domain → creates: "Customer Onboarding Data Flow View"
Applied to the Finance domain → creates: "Financial Reporting Data Flow View"

Each view is DIFFERENT (different content) but CONSISTENT (same notation, same concerns addressed, same level of detail) because they came from the same viewpoint.

Exam tip

A viewpoint is like a camera with a particular lens type. The camera type (viewpoint) stays the same, but each photograph (view) shows something different. One camera → many photographs.

Views — What They Formally Are

A View is:

  1. A specific representation of architecture — it shows real architecture content, not a template
  2. Created by applying a viewpoint — you don't create a view without first selecting a viewpoint
  3. Addresses specific concerns — it is designed to answer specific stakeholder questions
  4. Expressed as artifacts — diagrams, matrices, catalogs, tables

Views are NOT:

  • Generic diagrams created without stakeholder purpose
  • Random documentation
  • The same as a viewpoint

Does TOGAF Prescribe Specific Viewpoints?

No — TOGAF does NOT mandate a specific set of viewpoints that every organization must use. This is a deliberate design decision:

  • Different industries have different stakeholder needs
  • Different organizations have different governance requirements
  • Different projects require different views

TOGAF provides guidance and examples of viewpoints but expects organizations to:

  1. Identify their specific stakeholders and concerns
  2. Select or create viewpoints appropriate to those concerns
  3. Store useful viewpoints in the Architecture Repository (Reference Library) for future reuse

Over time, organizations build a Viewpoint Library — a collection of proven viewpoints that can be applied to future projects.

Exam tip

A common wrong answer is "TOGAF prescribes a specific set of viewpoints that all organizations must use." The correct answer: TOGAF provides guidance on viewpoints but does not prescribe a mandatory set. Organizations create their own viewpoints and store them for reuse.

Creating Architecture Views — The Full Process

When an architect needs to create a view for a specific stakeholder:

Step 1: Identify the Stakeholder and Concern "The CFO needs to understand the financial impact of the proposed application rationalization."

Step 2: Determine if an Existing Viewpoint Covers This Check the Architecture Repository Reference Library. Does a "Financial Impact Viewpoint" already exist?

  • If yes: retrieve and apply it
  • If no: create a new viewpoint and store it for future use

Step 3: Define or Select the Viewpoint Specify: what concerns it addresses, what notation it uses, what level of detail is appropriate, who the intended audience is.

Step 4: Apply the Viewpoint to the Architecture Draw on the Architecture Definition Document and specific architecture data to create the view. The view is specific to THIS architecture.

Step 5: Verify the View Addresses the Concern Review with the stakeholder: "Does this view answer your questions?"

Step 6: Store the View The view becomes part of the Architecture Definition Document. The viewpoint (the template) is stored in the Reference Library.

Once a viewpoint has been created and proven useful, it should be stored in the Reference Library (Layer 5) of the Architecture Repository. This enables:

Key Takeaway for Day 3 (Views and Viewpoints)

TOGAF does NOT prescribe a mandatory set of viewpoints — organizations create their own and store them in the Reference Library. Views address specific stakeholder concerns; creating the right views is how architecture is communicated effectively.

Day 5: Advanced ADM Techniques and Architecture Practice

Business Scenarios — Full Technique

Business Scenarios is the primary TOGAF-recommended technique for Phase A Architecture Vision development. Let's go deeper than the brief mention in Week 2.

What a Business Scenario Is

A Business Scenario is a complete description of a business problem (or opportunity) that the architecture must address. It tells the story of the problem from the perspective of the people affected.

TOGAF defines it as:

A technique that is used to describe a business need and the actors, systems, and other elements involved in achieving that need. Business Scenarios help to identify and understand the business requirements that an architecture must address.

The Components of a Business Scenario

A complete Business Scenario contains:

  1. Problem Description (the Problem Statement)

    • What is going wrong (or what opportunity exists)?
    • What are the business impacts?
    • Why is it a problem NOW?
    • Example: "Field engineers cannot access customer equipment histories when on-site, leading to repeat visits (25% of all service calls) and customer dissatisfaction."

  2. Business and Technical Environment

    • The context in which the problem exists
    • What systems, processes, and organizational structures are involved
    • What constraints exist (geographic, regulatory, budget)

  3. The Actors

    • Human Actors: The people involved (field engineers, dispatchers, customers, managers)
    • Computer Actors: The systems involved (Field Service Management system, ERP, customer database)
    • Note the distinction: both people AND systems are actors

  4. The Roles

    • What role does each actor play?
    • Which actors are primary (directly affected) vs. secondary (supporting)?

  5. The Desired Outcomes

    • What does success look like?
    • Specific, measurable improvements
    • Example: "Field engineers access complete equipment history in under 30 seconds from any location; repeat visits reduced by 80%; customer satisfaction score improves from 3.2 to 4.5"

  6. The Resulting Business Requirements

    • What must the architecture enable?
    • These requirements become inputs to the Architecture Requirements Specification

Business Scenarios Process (6 Steps)

  1. Identify, document, and rank the business goal that the scenario will address
  2. Identify the business and technical environment and document in models
  3. Identify and document desired outcomes as business objectives
  4. Identify human actors and computer actors and their roles
  5. Identify and document roles, responsibilities, and measures of success per actor
  6. Check for completeness and consistency — does the scenario cover all the elements?

Why Business Scenarios Drive Requirements

Business Scenarios are NOT just narrative stories. They systematically produce:

  • Business requirements (what the business needs to do differently)
  • Technical requirements (what the systems must support)
  • Data requirements (what information must be accessible)
  • Stakeholder concerns (what each actor cares about)

All of these feed directly into the Architecture Requirements Specification. This is why Business Scenarios are the recommended technique for Phase A — they ensure the architecture addresses real business needs, not just technical preferences.

Exam tip

Know the 6 components of a Business Scenario: Problem Description, Business/Technical Environment, Desired Outcomes, Human Actors, Computer Actors, and Resulting Requirements. Questions often ask "what are the actors in a Business Scenario?" — the answer includes BOTH human actors AND computer actors (systems).

Architecture Patterns — In Practice

An Architecture Pattern is a reusable solution to a recurring architecture problem.

Characteristics of Architecture Patterns

  • Named: Patterns have established names that architects recognize (e.g., "Hub-and-Spoke", "Event-Driven Architecture")
  • Proven: Patterns have been applied successfully in multiple organizations
  • Documented: A pattern is documented with: context, problem, solution, consequences, examples
  • Reusable: The same pattern can be applied to different organizations and different technology stacks
  • Technology-neutral: Patterns describe the architecture structure, not the specific technology

Describes HOW to organize components WHAT functional capability is needed

Example "Event-Driven Architecture" pattern "Message Broker Service" ABB → "Apache Kafka 3.x" SBB

A pattern can USE building blocks: the Event-Driven Architecture pattern uses a Message Broker ABB, an Event Publisher ABB, and an Event Subscriber ABB.

Security Architecture as a Cross-Cutting Concern

Security Architecture is special in TOGAF because it spans ALL four architecture domains — it is not confined to Technology Architecture:

Business Architecture Security Concerns:

  • Business continuity requirements (what must keep operating if systems fail)
  • Regulatory compliance obligations (GDPR, PCI-DSS, NCA Cybersecurity Framework in KSA)
  • Information classification policies (what is confidential, restricted, public)

Data Architecture Security Concerns:

  • Data classification (what data requires what level of protection)
  • Data sovereignty (where sensitive data can be stored geographically)
  • Encryption requirements for data at rest and in transit
  • Access control for data entities

Application Architecture Security Concerns:

  • Authentication and authorization within applications
  • Secure coding requirements
  • Application-to-application authentication (API security)
  • Security for specific high-risk applications

Technology Architecture Security Concerns:

  • Network security zones and firewalls
  • Infrastructure hardening standards
  • Security monitoring and SIEM
  • Identity and Access Management (IAM) platform

Security Architecture as Capability Architecture: In the Architecture Landscape, Security Architecture is often a Capability Architecture — a shared enabling architecture that cuts across all Segment Architectures. An enterprise-wide Security Architecture standard applies to every business unit and project.

This means:

  • Security Architecture is developed separately as a Capability Architecture
  • All Segment Architectures must be consistent with the Security Capability Architecture
  • The Security Capability Architecture uses TRM's "Security Services" layer as its technology foundation
Exam tip

Security is a cross-cutting concern that appears in all 4 architecture domains. It is an example of a Capability Architecture — an enabling architecture that applies across the whole enterprise. The TRM includes "Security Services" as a category within the Application Platform.

SOA in TOGAF Context

Service-Oriented Architecture (SOA) is an application architecture style where:

  • Business capabilities are exposed as services with well-defined interfaces
  • Services are loosely coupled (changes to one service don't break others)
  • Services communicate through standardized protocols (SOAP, REST, messaging)
  • Services can be composed into larger composite services

TOGAF Part III includes guidance on "Applying the TOGAF ADM in an SOA Context." This means using the standard ADM phases but with SOA-specific considerations:

ADM Phase SOA-Specific Focus
Phase B Identify business services that map to capabilities
Phase C Define service portfolio (what services exist), service contracts, service interfaces
Phase D Define the service infrastructure (ESB, API gateway, service registry)
Phase E Sequence service implementation by business value

Service Contract: In SOA, a service contract is the formal definition of: what the service does (operations), what data it accepts/returns (schema), how to call it (protocol), what guarantees it provides (SLA). This is distinct from but related to the TOGAF Architecture Contract.

Exam tip

For Level 1, know that TOGAF provides SOA guidelines and that SOA is an application architecture style supported by TOGAF. Service contracts in SOA and Architecture Contracts in TOGAF are different things, though the concept of formal agreements is common to both.

Architecture Skills Framework and Maturity Models (Part VII)

Part VII (Architecture Capability Framework) includes more than just the Architecture Board and governance. It also defines:

Architecture Skills Framework: A classification of the skills needed to be an effective enterprise architect:

  • Generic business skills (leadership, communication, negotiation)
  • IT general knowledge (technical understanding across domains)
  • Enterprise architecture skills (ADM application, modeling, patterns)
  • Domain skills (business, data, application, technology domain expertise)

This framework is used by organizations to:

  • Assess the skills of their architecture team
  • Identify training and development needs
  • Define job descriptions for architecture roles

Architecture Maturity Models: TOGAF references architecture capability maturity as a spectrum. Organizations progress from:

  • Level 0: No architecture (ad-hoc, no framework)
  • Level 1: Initial/ad-hoc architecture practice
  • Level 2: Developing architecture practice (some standards, some governance)
  • Level 3: Defined architecture practice (consistent methods, governance exists)
  • Level 4: Managed architecture practice (quantitative governance, metrics-driven)
  • Level 5: Optimizing architecture practice (continuous improvement, industry-leading)

The Preliminary Phase typically establishes where an organization currently sits on this maturity scale and defines the target maturity level.

Exam tip

For Level 1, know that architecture maturity models and skills frameworks exist in Part VII. You don't need detailed memorization — just know they exist and that they're used to establish and develop the EA capability.

Common Exam Traps and How to Avoid Them

Trap 1: "Transition Architecture is a Phase F output"

  • Wrong. Transition Architecture is defined in Phase E.
  • Phase F uses Transition Architectures as input for detailed migration planning.

Trap 2: "Architecture Contracts are created in Phase G"

  • Wrong. Architecture Contracts are created in Phase F.
  • Phase G enforces them.

Trap 3: "Phase C produces physical data models"

  • Wrong. Phase C produces logical data models (technology-independent).
  • Physical data models are created at project level during implementation.

Trap 4: "The Architecture Board designs architecture"

  • Wrong. The Architecture Board GOVERNS architecture — it approves, reviews, and arbitrates.
  • Architects DESIGN architecture.

Trap 5: "TOGAF prescribes specific mandatory viewpoints"

  • Wrong. TOGAF provides guidance on viewpoints but does not mandate specific ones.
  • Organizations create their own viewpoints.

Trap 6: "Gap Analysis is done in Phase E"

  • Wrong. Gap Analysis is done in Phases B, C, and D (one per domain).
  • Phase E CONSOLIDATES the gap analysis results from all three phases.

Trap 7: "The Statement of Architecture Work is an Architecture Contract"

  • Wrong. Statement of Architecture Work: Phase A output, governs architecture development.
  • Architecture Contract: Phase F output, governs implementation delivery.

Trap 8: "The Governance Log is Layer 5 of the Repository"

  • Wrong. Governance Log is Layer 6 (the deepest, most operational layer).
  • Layer 5 is the Reference Library.

Trap 9: "A View is a Template for Creating Views"

  • Wrong. A Viewpoint is the template. A View is the specific representation created from a viewpoint.

Trap 10: "Architecture Principles are established in Phase A"

  • Wrong. Architecture Principles are established in the Preliminary Phase.
  • Phase A confirms and refines them, but they originate in Preliminary.

The "Why" Behind TOGAF's Design

Understanding WHY TOGAF is designed the way it is helps you answer novel exam questions:

Why does the ADM have a Preliminary Phase before Phase A? Because setting up governance, principles, and the framework ONCE (in Preliminary) is more efficient than doing it for every project. Phase A benefits from the foundation Preliminary creates.

Why is Business Architecture designed before Data, Application, and Technology? Because technology exists to serve the business. You can't design the right data architecture without knowing what business processes need the data. Business drives all other domains.

Why is the Architecture Roadmap first complete in Phase E, not Phase F? Phase E is about consolidation — taking three separate domain gap analyses and creating a coherent integrated roadmap. Phase F is about operationalizing that roadmap (detailed planning). You need the complete picture before you can plan the details.

Why does Phase H loop back to different phases depending on change size? Because not every change needs a full architecture redesign (back to Phase A). Minor changes can be absorbed in Phase H. Medium changes may need re-planning (Phase E/F). Only major changes need full redesign. This efficiency principle avoids unnecessary work.

Why does TOGAF not prescribe mandatory viewpoints? Because different industries, organizations, and stakeholders have different concerns. A banking organization needs a Risk Architecture Viewpoint. A healthcare organization needs a Clinical Data Governance Viewpoint. A manufacturing company needs an Operational Technology Viewpoint. Mandating specific viewpoints would make TOGAF inflexible.

Why are Architecture Contracts created in Phase F (not G)? Because contracts must be in place BEFORE work begins. Phase G is implementation — contracts must be agreed and signed before implementation starts so that compliance can be measured against them from day one.

Key Takeaway for Day 6 (Synthesis)

All 7 parts of TOGAF form an integrated system: ADM (process), Content Framework (outputs), Enterprise Continuum (storage/classification), Governance (control), Techniques (tools), Reference Models (starting points), Introduction (vocabulary). Master the key distinctions — Phase E vs F, View vs Viewpoint, ABB vs SBB, TRM vs III-RM, etc. — and know the common exam traps. The "why" behind each design choice helps you answer novel questions.

A) Common Systems Architecture
B) Organization-Specific Architecture
C) Industry Architecture

Answer: D — Foundation Architecture is the most generic — it applies to ALL organizations. The continuum goes from most generic (Foundation) to most specific (Organization-Specific) as you move right.

A) Foundation Architecture
B) Common Systems Architecture
C) Industry Architecture
D) Organization-Specific Architecture

Answer: C — A banking industry reference architecture (like BIAN) represents the Industry Architecture level — it is specific to the banking sector but not to any single organization. A) The Architecture Continuum covers data and applications; the Solutions Continuum covers technology
B) The Architecture Continuum contains designs and reference architectures; the Solutions Continuum contains implementations, products, and systems
C) The Architecture Continuum is for large organizations; the Solutions Continuum is for small organizations
D) The Architecture Continuum is optional; the Solutions Continuum is mandatory

A) ADM Iteration
B) Architecture Partitioning
C) Enterprise Continuum classification
D) Architecture Governance escalation

Answer: B — Architecture Partitioning divides large enterprise architecture into segments (by level, domain, geography, or time horizon). A key rule of partitioning is that lower-level architectures (Segment, Capability) must be consistent with the higher-level Strategic Architecture.

A) Architecture Landscape (Layer 3)
B) Standards Information Base (Layer 4)
C) Reference Library (Layer 5)
D) Governance Log (Layer 6)

Answer: C — TRM and III-RM are Foundation Architecture reference models — they go in the Reference Library (Layer 5). The Architecture Landscape (Layer 3) stores organization-specific architectures. The Standards Information Base (Layer 4) stores approved standards. The Governance Log (Layer 6) stores governance decisions.

A) From Organization-Specific toward Foundation (right to left)
B) From Foundation toward Organization-Specific (left to right)
C) Reuse only flows between organizations at the same level

Answer: B — When CREATING an architecture, you look LEFT (from specific toward generic) to find what you can reuse. You START with Foundation Architecture, then add Common Systems patterns, then Industry patterns, then your specific customizations. This is the reuse direction: generic → specific.
